sections.title: The Anointing of David
observations: In this section, God instructs Samuel to anoint a new king, as Saul has been rejected due to his disobedience. This highlights God's sovereignty in choosing leaders according to His own criteria, rather than human standards.

Samuel's hesitance to go to Bethlehem reflects the gravity of the task, as anointing a new king could be seen as treasonous against Saul. Yet, God reassures him, emphasizing the importance of obedience to divine command.

sections.title: God's Choice of David
observations: As Samuel meets Jesse and his sons, he is initially impressed by Eliab, the eldest. However, God reminds him that He looks at the heart, not outward appearances. This teaches a profound lesson about God's perspective on leadership and character.
The selection of David, the youngest and least likely candidate, underscores the theme of God choosing the humble and the overlooked to fulfill His purposes.

sections.title: The Spirit of the Lord Departing from Saul
observations: After David is anointed, the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, while the Spirit departs from Saul. This transition signifies a shift in divine favor and the consequences of Saul's disobedience.
Saul's increasing distress and the introduction of David as a musician to soothe him illustrate the tension between the two kings and foreshadow the future conflict.

importantVerses.commentary: But the Lord said to Samuel, 'Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the Lord sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.'
Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon David from that day forward. And Samuel rose up and went to Ramah.

questions: What does God's choice of David teach us about His criteria for leadership?
How does the departure of the Spirit from Saul illustrate the consequences of disobedience?
In what ways can we apply the lesson of looking at the heart rather than outward appearances in our own lives?
